name: Satisfaction paradox
aliases: Paradox of the contented female worker
statement: Women report job satisfaction as high as or higher than men while holding jobs that pay less and offer less.
meaning: Two different findings travel under this name, and the entry has to pick one. In medicine the satisfaction paradox is Herschbach's observation that objectively negative circumstances have little effect on subjective quality of life, which the social sciences call the well-being paradox. This entry is about the other one, the labour-market finding usually called the paradox of the contented female worker. Its claim is narrower and easier to test. Women are paid less, promoted less and report more discrimination at work, and they still rate their jobs at least as highly as men rate theirs. The gap survives controls for the jobs people actually hold, so it is not produced by men and women doing different work. Andrew Clark's account is that satisfaction measures the distance between a job and what the worker expected of it, and that women expected less because women had held worse jobs in the past. That account carries a prediction. As women's position in the labour market improves and expectations converge on men's, the gap should shrink and then vanish.

origin.note: Crosby's book Relative Deprivation and Working Women gave the pattern its name. Clark's 1997 paper in Labour Economics established it in economics and supplied the expectations account, and Hodson had asked the same question in The Sociological Quarterly in 1989. The Crosby attribution is quoted from Brüggemann and Hinz, who write that the finding 'was termed the "paradox of the contented female worker" by Crosby (1982)'. The book itself was not obtained.

evidence: Clark's paper could not be obtained, so what it did is reported here from two later papers that use it. Vladisavljević and Perugini write that Clark grouped the candidate explanations into five sets, differences in individual and job characteristics, differences in work values, selection bias, differences in relative income distributions and differences in expectations, and found the first four insufficient. They also record his finding that no significant gender gap appeared among younger workers, highly educated workers, workers whose mothers had professional jobs, workers in professional or managerial posts, and workers in male-dominated workplaces. Green, Heywood, Kler and Leeves report Clark's adjusted 1991 gap as 0.240 satisfaction points. Later work does not agree on whether the pattern is still there. Vladisavljević and Perugini used the 2013 EU-SILC well-being module for 32 European countries, with job satisfaction on an eleven-point scale, and found a pooled female advantage of 0.058 points on a matched sample. The country-level picture is split. The female advantage reached significance in seven countries, Portugal, the United Kingdom, Iceland, Malta, the Netherlands, Cyprus and Hungary, while men were significantly more satisfied in Croatia, Bulgaria, Slovakia and Poland. Redmond and McGuinness used the 2014 European Skills and Jobs Survey, which covers 48,000 workers in 28 EU countries. A female advantage survived their personal, job and family controls. It disappeared once nine job preferences were added, with work-life balance and intrinsic interest doing most of the work. Brüggemann and Hinz turned the question to pay fairness, using round 9 of the European Social Survey from 2018. Their sample is 13,544 respondents in 752 occupations across 27 countries, each rating their own gross pay from extremely unfairly low to extremely unfairly high. Women rated their pay less fair than men, by 0.251 scale points raw and 0.139 with controls, and the raw coefficient ran that way in 23 of the 27 countries. Dilmaghani studied the Canadian General Social Survey for 2016. Her abstract reports a female advantage that holds in the aggregate and falls to insignificance among the youngest and most educated workers. Once subjective intrinsic rewards are controlled for it reverses in favour of men among holders of graduate degrees.

examples.tag: The staff survey that answers itself twice
examples.text: A department's survey shows women rating pay and prospects lower than men, and rating overall satisfaction with the job as high or higher. Both answers come from the same questionnaire, so the paradox sits on one page rather than being assembled across studies.

examples.tag: Two people on the same grade
examples.text: A man and a woman on identical terms are asked how satisfied they are. She has been passed over twice and still rates the job well, because she is measuring it against the jobs she has held before rather than against the one he holds.

A woman entering a profession her mother was kept out of arrives expecting the pay and the promotions. She reports less satisfaction on better terms than her mother reported on worse ones, because the standard the job is measured against has risen.

replication.headline: Clark's 1991 British estimate reproduces on his own data source, and the gap in that series is gone by 2012 to 2014, while studies in other countries and on other measures disagree about whether it survives anywhere.
replication.detail: Green, Heywood, Kler and Leeves re-estimated Clark's specification on the British Household Panel Survey and its successor, Understanding Society. The panel is unbalanced and holds 22,328 individuals, and job satisfaction is a seven-point scale. Table 1 of the published article puts the raw female advantage in 1991 at 0.301 satisfaction points, though the text beside it says 0.305. The advantage adjusted for individual and job characteristics was 0.242, against the 0.240 they report from Clark. By 2008 the raw figure was 0.189 and the adjusted figure 0.108, and the table marks both significant at the 1 per cent level. For the pooled years 2012 to 2014 the raw figure was 0.005 and the adjusted figure 0.027, neither distinguishable from zero. Mean female satisfaction fell from near 5.7 in the early years to the 5.2 to 5.3 band, while men sat between 5.1 and 5.3 throughout. An Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition gives the coefficients 0.422 of the 1991 raw difference of 0.400, and the characteristics minus 0.022, so the coefficients carry more than the whole of it. By 2012 to 2014 the raw gap is 0.013 and the characteristics now favour women: their jobs did not get worse, they judged them more harshly. The authors write that very few of the yearly estimates from 2006 to 2015 differ from zero at the 5 per cent level. These figures come from the accepted version of the 2018 article, deposited by NTNU in the Norwegian national research archive and read in full. The 2016 Lancaster University Management School working paper, titled 'Paradox Lost: Disappearing Female Job Satisfaction', runs the same exercise on data stopping in 2012 and prints different numbers, among them an adjusted 1991 gap of 0.234 and an adjusted 2012 gap of 0.009.

study.cite: Green, C. P., Heywood, J. S., Kler, P., & Leeves, G. (2018). Paradox Lost: The Disappearing Female Job Satisfaction Premium. British Journal of Industrial Relations, 56(3), 484-502.

limits: Clark's paper was not obtained, on 21 September 2026. ScienceDirect returned 403 to two user agents, Crossref carries no abstract for it, and Unpaywall, OpenAlex and OpenAIRE list no open copy anywhere. The Kingston University record holds no file, the 1993 Essex discussion paper of the same title offers no download through RePEc, and Clark's own page at the Paris School of Economics lists the citation without a file. Every figure credited to Clark on this page is quoted from a paper that cites him, and none of it went into the structured fields. Green and colleagues state that their evidence uses Clark's original data source and is unique to the United Kingdom, and they decline to claim the trend extends beyond it. The published version puts that caution differently from the working paper. It notes that early evidence placed the paradox most clearly in Anglo-Saxon countries, but that Hauret and Williams find the female advantage most evident in Nordic ones. The studies gathered here are not repeats of one another. Overall job satisfaction, satisfaction with pay and the perceived fairness of one's own wage are three different measures, and only the British series re-estimates the original specification on the original data. Vladisavljević and Perugini contradict themselves once, in their conclusion. Their tables print the interaction of female with early-life gender equality as minus 0.465 and their results section reads it as negative, which means early equality narrows the gap. One sentence of the conclusion says instead that early exposure to equality is connected to higher female job satisfaction, and the summary two paragraphs later says the opposite again. Dilmaghani's paper was read only in the abstract Wiley supplies through Crossref. The full text was tried again and refused, Wiley returning 403 and the Saint Mary's University repository returning 403 from its server rather than a paywall. Crosby's book of 1982 and Hodson's paper of 1989 were not read, and the publisher and year in the origin field come from an Open Library catalogue record. The published 2019 Labour Economics version of the Vladisavljević and Perugini working paper was not read either. The Belgrade Institute of Economic Sciences lists an accepted copy, but its file answers 401, and the Perugia repository could not be reached from here. None of the studies read here measures workers' expectations directly. Clark's own account of the mechanism, as Vladisavljević and Perugini describe it, was indirect, resting on age, education and occupation as proxies that 'might be realistically correlated with expectations'.
misreadings: The name is the first trap. Herschbach's paper reports that the phenomenon 'has been called paradoxical' in two literatures at once, and that 'in medicine it is called the "satisfaction paradox" and in the social sciences the "well-being paradox"'. What is meant there is that objectively negative factors in a life have relatively little effect on subjective quality of life. That is a claim about illness, disability and hardship, and it is not the claim about women's jobs. Nothing on this page bears on it. The stronger version, that people in bad conditions are about as satisfied as anyone else, is contested for life satisfaction. Veenhoven writes that people are typically dissatisfied when they live in miserable conditions, that dissatisfaction is the rule in poor third world countries, and that in western nations life satisfaction is lower where adverse conditions accumulate. The disappearance of the British gap is read as a refutation of Clark, and it is closer to the opposite. He predicted that the paradox would be temporary, and Green and colleagues call their result largely consistent with that prediction. Nor was the pattern ever universal. In the 2013 EU-SILC data men were the more satisfied sex in several countries of eastern Europe. The finding is also used to argue that women's jobs are therefore acceptable. Clark's account says the reverse, that the satisfaction was a record of low expectations formed by a poor labour-market position.
